clue.text: Rollmop — who rants when it's badly served?

definitions.text: Rollmop — who rants when it's badly served?

indicators.note: something badly served is dished up all wrong, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A diner fumes at a pickled herring that arrives poorly presented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly served' rearranges the fifteen letters of ROLLMOP and WHO RANTS. The whole clue is also the definition: Antony Worrall Thompson is a British TV chef, just the man to rant at a badly served dish.
explanation.definitionFit: The chef Antony Worrall Thompson, known from British television cookery, is pictured as the diner fuming over a poorly plated rollmop.

clue.text: Indian bringing up child, say, on nothing

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it
in a down clue, bringing words up means writing them from the bottom upwards, so they read backwards

parts.note: a minor is a child in law
EG, for example, is what 'say' means
O is the figure nought

explanation.surface: A Native American raises a child who will one day be worth nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bringing up' turns MINOR and EG together, giving GERONIM; 'on' sets that above O.
explanation.definitionFit: Geronimo was a famous Apache leader, an example of a Native American, which older crosswords call an Indian.

clue.text: Line in game — a Cockney game, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a word spoken, so the letters entered match the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: Cockneys, Londoners from the East End, drop their H, so hockey is said 'ockey

explanation.surface: Someone describes a marking on a pitch in a sport, comparing it with an East London pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: In darts the oche is the line players stand behind to throw, so it is a line in a game.

clue.text: What's the matter with setter? Just a menial!

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog; here it is possessive, the dog's
body means physical matter, substance

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is wrong with the crossword compiler, who is only a lowly drudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like the puzzle's compiler, but it is the dog; 'What's the matter with setter?' reads as 'the dog's body'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogsbody is a British term for a person given all the menial, boring jobs, so it names a menial.

clue.text: Complaint when lousy maths gets the top grade

indicators.note: lousy means very poor, so the word is reworked into a different order

parts.note: A is the highest exam grade

explanation.surface: A pupil grumbles that poor arithmetic still earned the best mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma is a medical condition, and a complaint is an illness or ailment.

clue.text: Hesitation about male couple, one showing amorousness?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the others

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitating
a brace is a pair, used of game birds

explanation.surface: A pause around two men suggests one of them is feeling affectionate.
explanation.definitionFit: An embracer is someone who hugs, a person showing affection or amorousness.

clue.text: Get rid of one ring? More than one

parts.note: to annul is to cancel or abolish
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone wants to discard a ring, then wonders whether there are several.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition asks for the plural of a ring: one annulus, several annuli.
explanation.definitionFit: Annuli is the plural of annulus, a ring-shaped figure, so it means more than one ring.

clue.text: Garden is this possible worry to health and safety people

definitions.text: possible worry to health and safety people

parts.note: the letters of this word could be rearranged, potentially, into another word meaning peril

explanation.surface: A safety inspector worries that a garden could be hazardous.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: POTENTIAL is an anagram signal and DANGER rearranges to GARDEN, the clue's first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A potential danger is a possible hazard, the sort of risk safety officers look out for.

clue.text: What's missing here on each mule, for example

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what is absent from every mule.
explanation.walkthrough: This grid has no entry numbered 1 across, so the clue points to that gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle's numbering skips the first across slot, so that entry is literally what is missing from the grid.

clue.text: Fruit with which chap gets energy

parts.note: a chap is a man
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: Someone asks what fruit gives a man his get-up-and-go.
explanation.definitionFit: A mango is a tropical fruit, an example of the fruit category.

clue.text: People behaving badly, endlessly brusque after port

indicators.note: after places the trimmed word behind the port

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port

indicators.note: endlessly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: terse means curt or brusque

explanation.surface: Sailors misbehave, being constantly rude once they have left a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' removes the final E of TERSE, leaving TERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioters are members of a disorderly mob, people behaving badly in public.

clue.text: Detective — the man with right key to mystery, but confused inside

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a man

indicators.note: the middle of the word is muddled, so its inner letters swap places

parts.note: a clue is a key to solving a mystery

explanation.surface: A sleuth arrives with the vital evidence but is muddled in his thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused inside' muddles only the two middle letters, leaving the first and last in place; 'the man' is the usual crossword way of giving HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercule Poirot is Agatha Christie's Belgian detective, known by his first name.

clue.text: Girl seen with floosies regularly

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter, here the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: A young woman is often spotted in the company of loose women.
explanation.definitionFit: Lois is a girl's name, an example of a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Cast-iron HM fan

indicators.note: to fan is to spread out, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is a steadfast supporter of Her Majesty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' looks like the noun supporter, but as a verb it spreads out the letters of CAST-IRON HM; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarchist supports rule by a king or queen, so a firm admirer of Her Majesty is one.

clue.text: Communist hack's movement against organisation dominated by Murdoch?

parts.note: a hack is a riding horse, and a trot is one of its paces
Sky, the broadcaster, was controlled by Rupert Murdoch's media empire

explanation.surface: A left-wing journalist campaigns against the Murdoch press empire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' wants to be a journalist; it is a horse. 'against' just sets the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Leon Trotsky was a leading Russian revolutionary, a famous communist.

clue.text: Commercial in newspaper and women's mag for summer item

parts.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

indicators.note: in puts the advert inside the magazine's name

parts.note: She was a British women's magazine
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: An advert for a summer product runs in a tabloid and a women's magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunshade, such as a parasol or awning, is used in summer to keep off the sun.

clue.text: Female once at an inn and held by male terrorists

indicators.note: held by means placed inside the other pieces

parts.note: the IRA, the Irish Republican Army, was a paramilitary group

explanation.surface: A woman at a pub is seized by a man from a terrorist group.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls Hilaire Belloc's poem Tarantella: 'Do you remember an Inn, Miranda?'
explanation.definitionFit: Belloc's poem addresses a woman who once stayed at an inn, so the definition names her.

clue.text: Fellow to block the Guardian with legal order

parts.note: a fellow is a man
to dam is to block a flow
the clue appeared in the Guardian, so the paper speaking of itself is us

explanation.surface: A man tries to stop the newspaper using a court injunction.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandamus is a writ from a higher court ordering a body to do its duty, a legal order.

clue.text: Written marks in old books held by the state

indicators.note: held by means the books go inside the state

parts.note: a nation is a state
OT is the Old Testament

explanation.surface: Ancient volumes are kept by the government.
explanation.definitionFit: Notation is a system of written symbols, such as musical marks.

clue.text: Winning with a beer belly?

definitions.meaning: having a stomach that bulges forward, said playfully

explanation.definitionFit: A leader in a race is ahead of the others, and a paunch sticks forward from the body.

clue.text: Rock collector rummaging among rubbish

definitions.meaning: a British rag-and-bone man or scavenger who goes 'totting', picking over rubbish

explanation.definitionFit: To totter is to sway or rock, and in British slang a totter scavenges refuse for saleable items.

clue.text: Try again to work out setter

indicators.note: to work something out is to rearrange it into a solution, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler is told to have another go at solving.
explanation.definitionFit: To retest is to try or examine again.

clue.text: Boss with less than what it takes to get an MBA?

indicators.note: less than the full word means one letter is dropped from its end

parts.words: what it takes to get an MBA
parts.note: earning a business degree takes study

explanation.surface: A manager wonders whether he has done less than enough work for a business degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like a manager, but it is a raised ornament or knob.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a stud, an ornamental knob or projection on a surface.

clue.text: Remark about dish fresh from the oven amounts to criticism

parts.note: a pot is a cooking dish; with 's it reads as 'pot is'
food just out of the oven is hot

explanation.surface: A cook's warning that a dish is hot is taken as a dig.
explanation.walkthrough: The remark is 'pot's hot', run together as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A potshot is a random or sniping criticism.

clue.text: Is French in a leading position? It's a language that's faded!

indicators.note: in puts the French word inside the phrase

parts.note: A plus van, the vanguard or leading position
est is French for is

explanation.surface: Someone asks if French still leads, then calls it a fading tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Avestan is an ancient Iranian language of Zoroastrian scripture, long dead.

clue.text: Pound for a book

definitions.meaning: a book of the Old Testament

explanation.definitionFit: The American poet Pound had this first name, and it is also an Old Testament book title.

clue.text: Love to look at a nymph

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O
to read is to look at text

explanation.surface: Someone loves to gaze at a nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: An oread is a mountain nymph in Greek mythology.

clue.text: No trendy individual is beginning here in the NW

parts.note: a square is someone old-fashioned, not trendy
one means a single individual

explanation.surface: An unfashionable person sets off from the north-west.
explanation.walkthrough: The first numbered square of a grid sits in its top-left, or north-west, corner, where you begin.
explanation.definitionFit: Square one is the starting point, and in this grid it is the top-left cell.
